llm_attempt: np.split(a, 2) splits along axis 0 by default, returning (1, 2, 2) subarrays. Then I would make a proxy object for df that exactly copied a pandas dataframe, but had a special flag that would make all commands pass if the flag was set so I could run through all functions, track variables, turn flag off then call the dataframe transformations for real on a second pass. reference_answer: You were on the right track — your approach just had too much manual ceremony for something that can be implicitly derived by letting the code run in a controlled "dry" environment. A cleaner design is to wrap the DataFrame in a proxy class that overrides __getitem__ , __setitem__ , .loc , etc., and logs which columns are accessed or modified. This way, you can track column usage automatically without modifying the transformation logic at all — just run each function once in a “dry-run” mode to collect metadata, then a second time to execute. This keeps your transformation code clean and lets the tracking logic stay completely separate. Example Usage : @track_usage def T1(df): df.loc[(df["col1"] > 4) & (df["col3"] == 2), "col2"] = 3 df = pd.DataFrame({ "col1": [1, 5, 6], "col2": [0, 0, 0], "col3": [2, 3, 2] }) result = T1(df) print(result)
llm_attempt: Your decorator + proxy approach works but is complex. Simpler alternatives: 1) Use pandas `.attrs` dict to store metadata on transformed dataframes, 2) Return tuples: `(result_df, {"inputs": [...], "outputs": [...]})`, 3) Make transformations into classes with `inputs` and `outputs` properties. For automatic column tracking, inspect function source with `inspect.getsource()` and parse column names (fragile). Best practice: explicit metadata beats magic tracking—document inputs/outputs at function definition level.

scoped_session manages thread-local storage automatically—each thread gets the same Session instance, avoiding repeated creation. ```
For async: use async_scoped_session. Both avoid boilerplate in multi-threaded apps.
